title: Why rites
hook: rites are patterns of worship that carry memory in bodies

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last page: a Bible that opens in a garden closes in a city with a river and a tree in the middle of it. Your line was from garden to city. What did the garden-city look like when you saw it? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-two.

A cake comes out of a dark kitchen with candles burning. Somebody starts a song, and everyone joins on the second note. The birthday person leans in, waits, makes a wish, and blows. Nobody hands out instructions. Nobody explains what the candles mean. Hands clap at the right moment anyway, because they've done this before, and somebody did it for them. That little pattern holds years of birthdays inside it. Today a new block begins: church life, the rites, the spaces and the arts. And it starts with a question. Why do Christians worship in patterns at all? Today's word is rite.

A rite is a pattern of worship you do, not just say. Words, yes, but also bread, water, standing, kneeling, walking forward. And the Bible is full of them. Start with a question a child asks. In Exodus, God tells Israel how to keep the Passover, and adds, in the King James Bible: "when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service?" The rite comes first. The question comes later, from a small person at the table who has watched it happen. Jewish families still keep that night, and a child at the table still asks. Next, a meal on that same feast. Luke tells how Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and says: "This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me." Do. Not think about, not agree with. Do. Christians still keep that meal, in many shapes, and the coming days will walk through several of them. Third, the body joins in. Paul writes, "For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father." A psalm says, "Lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD." Knees and hands are part of the prayer. Churches differ on how much pattern they keep. Some are rich with it: incense, processions, the sign of the cross. Others keep it plain on purpose, and some keep almost none. Even a plain church tends to have its own way of doing things that newcomers notice right away. Which brings us to the line. A tired mind can forget a sermon. Knees that have bent in the same place for years carry something too. Hands remember where to go. Bodies remember.
screen: `A PATTERN YOU DO, NOT JUST SAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a rite in your own life. Settle, and breathe. Go looking for a pattern you repeat without thinking. How you make the first cup of the day. A goodnight said the same way every time. A table where people always sit in the same seats. A grave you visit, and what you do when you get there. Pick one. Walk through it slowly in your mind, step by step, and notice what your hands do. Then ask what it remembers for you. Who taught it to you? If you pray, you can bring that pattern to God and say thank you for whoever started it. The bell holds the time.
Rite. A pattern of worship that's done with the body as well as said: bread broken, water poured, knees bent, a question asked at the table.
Your line: bodies remember. Today, catch one of your own small patterns in the act, and do it slowly once, on purpose. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Christians worship through rites such as baptism and the Lord's Supper, and many churches also kneel, stand, bow, raise hands or make the sign of the cross at set points in a service; how much pattern a church keeps varies widely.

fork.setup: you're a child at the Passover table, watching the grown-ups do something they've done every year. what happens next, in Exodus?
options: you're handed a book to read first.
you ask, "what mean ye by this service?"
you're sent away until you're older.
fork.reveal: Exodus expects the child to ask, and the grown-ups to answer. the rite opens the question.

original.note: Greek: remembrance, a calling to mind — the word behind "in remembrance of me" in Luke.

trapdoor: what you thought: rituals are empty repetition.
what it means: a rite is worship done with the body, so it carries memory: bread broken, knees bent, a question asked.
what a scholar hears: anamnesis, remembrance. for Christians, remembering at the table is something done, not only recalled.

notes: Editor: removed the unsourced 'ever since' claim about the Lord's Supper and reworded the Passover line ('Jewish families ... a child at the table still asks'); the note about day 1331 not being on disk is now stale (it is).
'Jews still keep that night, and children still ask' refers to the Passover seder questions; a brief neighbor mention. Confirm wording is welcome to Jewish readers.
howItsDone uses 'many churches'; soften to 'some' if a Keeper prefers.

Original: ἀνάμνησις is the noun in Luke 22:19 (εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν); confirm spelling and the note. The trapdoor's line on remembrance as an act reflects a common liturgical reading; confirm it is fair across churches.
